summaries.example: Imagine a map of a city. A map helps you notice streets and neighborhoods, but it is not the city itself. Philosophers say a model of what is ultimate works in a similar way: it helps us think about something very important and hard to examine directly.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what people mean when they talk about God and other ultimates. An ultimate is supposed to be the deepest reality, the highest value, the source of the greatest fulfillment, or some combination of these. Different traditions use names such as God, Brahman, and the Dao, but they do not all mean the same thing by those names. Even people within one tradition may disagree. The entry calls these ways of thinking models. A model is useful because it points toward something difficult to examine, but it is also limited and can leave things out. The entry explains that studying many models can help us avoid a quick mistake: rejecting one model does not prove that no other kind of ultimate exists. It also introduces ways to sort models, such as whether the ultimate is one with the world, includes the world, is part of the world, or is separate from it. Some thinkers welcome this variety, while others see it as a reason for caution or silence.
key_ideas: People in different religions and philosophies have different ideas about what is most real, most valuable, or most fulfilling.
Words such as God, Brahman, and the Dao can have many different models, even within the traditions that use them.
A model is not an exact copy. It shows some features and leaves out others.
Some people think there is nothing ultimate, while others think the idea is important to study before deciding.
Models can describe the ultimate as one with the world, larger than the world, part of the world, or separate from the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand why people can disagree about God or reality without discussing exactly the same idea. It also encourages careful listening across cultures and religions. Thinking about models can make our own beliefs more thoughtful and less hurried, while leaving open the question of whether anything ultimate really exists.

important_terms.definition: The state of being most deeply real, valuable, or able to bring the greatest fulfillment.
A way of describing or representing something, especially something we cannot inspect directly.
The view that there is one basic reality or one basic kind of thing.
The view that the world is part of what is ultimate, while the ultimate is larger than the world.

questions_to_think_about: Can people from different cultures share an idea without meaning exactly the same thing?
Can a model help us think about something that may be beyond ordinary experience?
If one idea of God is rejected, does that show that every idea of what is ultimate is wrong?
Would you rather study many possible models or choose one model quickly?

summaries.example: Suppose a student rejects an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good personal God because of an argument from suffering. The entry warns that this would target a particular model. It would not by itself disprove a non-personal ultimate, a God understood differently, or another account of what is most fundamental or fulfilling.
summaries.summary: “God and Other Ultimates” develops a framework for comparing ideas of what is ultimate across religions, philosophies, and quasi-religious philosophies. The entry proposes a cross-cultural core broad enough to include diverse cases: an ultimate is what is most fundamental in reality, has unsurpassable value, or provides the deepest kind of fulfillment. It loosens the requirement that all three features must be present, since some models emphasize only certain forms of ultimacy. This account is not neutral in every respect: it inherits concepts associated with perfect-being approaches and may not fit every tradition. The entry therefore stresses both shared humanity and genuine cultural difference. A model is a purposeful representation of a target that is difficult to examine directly. Models can organize thought and disclose patterns, but they are not copies and remain open to error. The project faces three broad challenges: perhaps nothing ultimate exists; perhaps the concept of ultimacy is incoherent; or perhaps human language and cognition cannot reach what is ultimate. Responses include silence, indirect or negative language, distinctions between an ultimate in itself and as experienced, and comparative study. The entry then classifies models by their relation to the world: monism or pantheism identifies the ultimate with the world, panentheism places the world within a larger ultimate, merotheism places the ultimate within a larger world, and dualism distinguishes the two. Its examples show that traditions contain internal disagreement as well as striking cross-traditional parallels.
key_ideas: The entry uses a deliberately flexible account of ultimacy: the ultimate may be most real, most valuable, deepest in fulfillment, or some combination, provided nothing else in the relevant system exceeds it.
There is disagreement about whether ultimacy has a shared cross-cultural core. Some emphasize cultural differences; others think comparison is possible if the category remains sufficiently open.
Models are conceptually distant from their targets. They are informative but fallible, and they may be concepts, metaphors, or indirect signs.
The existence of many models matters philosophically. Arguments against one model cannot automatically establish that nothing ultimate exists.
Models differ in their relation to the world. The main categories include monism or pantheism, panentheism, merotheism, and dualism.
The entry surveys models associated with Brahman, God, and the Dao, showing both disagreement within traditions and similarities across traditions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The framework matters because philosophical arguments often depend on which model they address. It also clarifies debates about religious diversity, religious language, meaning, and the possibility of knowledge about reality as a whole. Studying models does not settle whether an ultimate exists, but it can make that question more precise and prevent overgeneralizing from one conception to all conceptions.

important_terms.definition: A condition of being, or a feature of something, that makes it most fundamental, most valuable, or the deepest source of fulfillment.
A representation of a target that highlights some features for a purpose rather than copying the target exactly.
Ultimacy concerning the most fundamental fact about how things are.
Ultimacy concerning unsurpassable value or greatness.
Ultimacy concerning the source of liberation, salvation, or the deepest good sought by practitioners.
The view that the ultimate is identical with the world, or that there is only one basic reality.
The view that the world is within the ultimate, while the ultimate is more than the world.
The claim that ultimate reality cannot be adequately expressed or understood in ordinary human language or thought.

questions_to_think_about: Does a cross-cultural concept need a single defining essence, or can it be a family-resemblance category?
Are metaphysical, axiological, and soteriological ultimacy jointly necessary, or can one or two be sufficient?
Does the diversity of models count against the possibility of knowledge, or does it reveal different perspectives on a complex target?
Can statements about how an ultimate relates to the world be meaningful even if its inner nature is unknowable?
What standards should be used to compare models: coherence, moral adequacy, fit with science, non-anthropomorphism, or something else?

summaries.example: Think about a video-game world. One player might say the game is made by a creator outside it. Another might say the creator is present throughout the game. A third might say the whole game itself is the creator. These are different models of how an ultimate might relate to the world; none should be assumed to be the only possible model.
summaries.summary: This entry studies how people have thought about God and other possible ultimates. “Ultimate” is a broad philosophical idea: it concerns what is most real, most valuable, most fulfilling, or some combination of these. Names such as Brahman, God, and the Dao are used in different traditions, but each name may have several meanings. This makes comparison difficult. Some scholars argue that these traditions are separate cultural worlds and that imposing one definition can distort them. Others think comparison is possible because traditions and cultures have interacted and because human beings share important features. The entry therefore favors a category with enough shared meaning to be useful but enough openness to respect difference. It calls a way of thinking about an ultimate a model. Models are like maps: they represent a target for a purpose and reveal some relationships while simplifying others. The entry discusses three challenges. Someone may think nothing ultimate exists; someone else may argue that the idea itself is inconsistent; and another may say that the ultimate is beyond human language or knowledge. Possible responses include speaking indirectly, describing how the ultimate affects the world rather than what it is in itself, or treating spiritual experience as a different kind of evidence. Finally, models can be organized by their world relationship. Pantheism identifies the ultimate with the world, panentheism places the world within a larger ultimate, merotheism makes the ultimate part of the world, and dualism separates ultimate and world. The entry’s larger lesson is that disagreement within traditions and similarities across traditions are both important.
key_ideas: The entry compares ideas named God, Brahman, and the Dao, while emphasizing that each name can represent several different models.
A cross-cultural idea of ultimacy must be broad enough to include differences, but not so broad that it becomes meaningless.
The three useful dimensions of ultimacy are metaphysical, axiological, and soteriological: deepest reality, highest value, and deepest fulfillment or liberation.
Models help people reason about difficult subjects, but they are not perfect pictures. They can be useful and humble at the same time.
Some people challenge the project because nothing ultimate may exist, the concept may be incoherent, or human beings may not be able to describe the ultimate.
The variety of models can lead people to reject the whole project, learn from several traditions, hold beliefs more loosely, or compare models using standards such as coherence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Learning this framework helps us avoid treating “God,” “religion,” or “reality” as if each had only one obvious meaning. It supports fair comparison and better arguments. It also shows why philosophical care is needed: a criticism may defeat one model without defeating every possible account of what is most real, valuable, or fulfilling.

important_terms.definition: Being the deepest reality, highest value, deepest source of fulfillment, or a combination of these.
A representation used to think about a target that cannot be examined directly; it shows some aspects and leaves out others.
The philosophical study of what exists and what is most fundamental.
The study of value, including what is good, important, or excellent.
The view that the world and the ultimate are one reality or one basic kind of reality.
The view that the world is in the ultimate, but the ultimate is greater than the world.
The view that the ultimate is separate from the world, so there are two fundamentally different realities or kinds of reality.
A claim that something is beyond complete description or understanding through ordinary words and concepts.

questions_to_think_about: Why might cultural differences make a shared definition of ultimacy difficult?
Does rejecting one model of God give us enough reason to reject every model of ultimacy?
How can a model be useful if it is not an exact copy?
What is gained, and what might be lost, by describing the Dao or another ultimate through indirect language?
Should different traditions be judged by the same philosophical categories?
